content.overview: A deviation is a departure from an expected process, condition or result. Professional response begins by containing immediate risk, defining what actually happened and identifying affected material or records before deciding consequence.

vocabulary.definition: Immediate action that limits further impact while investigation continues.
The material, time period, equipment, records or people plausibly influenced by the event.
Documented decision governing the status or next step for affected material.

sections.title: Record facts before theories
sections.body: Capture event time, location, process version, observed condition and affected IDs before the scene changes.

sections.title: Use genealogy to limit uncertainty
sections.body: Traceable crop and post-harvest records help identify which lots were actually exposed instead of placing unrelated material under indefinite uncertainty.

sections.title: Consequence depends on evidence
sections.body: Duration, measurement quality and product/process knowledge determine whether an excursion is inconsequential, requires additional evaluation or supports hold/disposition.

workedExamples: A one-room sensor failure should be scoped to the period and lots connected to that room before assuming facility-wide impact.
A sanitation step missed on one batch can trigger containment of connected material while evidence is reviewed.
commonMistakes: Closing the record without affected-lot scope.
content.practicalApplication: Use a deviation form with event, immediate action, affected IDs, evidence, cause hypotheses, disposition and follow-up ownership.
content.summary: Professional deviation handling separates containment, investigation, scope and disposition so decisions are traceable.
